name: Harmon & Loomis's Store
aka: the Clark and South Water store building

documented_range.note: THE START IS THE FIRST DATE A SOURCE PUTS THE FIRM IN BUSINESS, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME AS PUTTING THE BUILDING IN EXISTENCE, and this range does not pretend otherwise. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries a display advertisement headed 'C. & I. HARMON', dated 18 November 1833, offering dry goods, crockery, hardware, wet and dry groceries and 'on commission, a large lot of Leather, Saddlery, &c.' — contemporary proof that a Harmon store was trading at Chicago three weeks before the town was a month into having a newspaper. Andreas independently lists 'Jim Kinzie's store, P. F. W. Peck's store, Harmon's and Loomis's' as all being on South Water Street by 1833. NEITHER STATEMENT DATES THE BUILDING. The corner attribution comes from a later Andreas passage describing the three-storey building at Clark and South Water that housed the Daily Chicago American on its third floor in 1839, and whether the 1835 building was that building, or its predecessor on the same lot, is unattested. THE END IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY CUT AT THE SCENE YEAR, not a demolition date.

change_note: The store building of Harmon and Loomis at the corner of Clark and South Water, trading through the mid-1830s: dry goods, crockery, hardware, wet and dry groceries, and leather and saddlery taken on commission. In 1839 a three-storey building on this corner carried the Daily Chicago American on its top floor; whether that was this building grown or a replacement is unattested, and the 1835 record deliberately takes none of its height.

placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE JUNCTION IS ATTESTED AND THE CORNER IS THIS RECORD'S CHOICE, ARGUED HERE RATHER THAN ASSUMED. Andreas gives 'corner of Clark and South Water' and never a side. Two of the four corners fall away on the dossier's own evidence: the north side of South Water was the river frontage, wharves and landings (docs/research/04-structures-south.md § 12), so the building is south of the street. That leaves south-west and south-east. THE SOUTH-WEST IS SEPARATELY AND EXPLICITLY CLAIMED: Andreas puts the Chicago Democrat's building on the south-west corner of the same junction, and the Democrat's own first issue confirms the junction from a contemporary imprint. This record therefore takes the south-east, and the reasoning is that two attested premises on one crossing are better modelled as two buildings on two corners than as one building asserted twice — but that is a modelling choice, not evidence, AND THE HONEST ALTERNATIVE IS THAT THEY WERE ONE BUILDING. Andreas says Calhoun 'secured an office IN a building' at this junction, i.e. he rented; Harmon & Loomis owned a building at this junction; a newspaper renting an office in a merchant's corner store is the ordinary arrangement of the period. IF THAT IS RIGHT, THIS RECORD STANDS ABOUT 37 M EAST OF WHERE IT BELONGS AND DUPLICATES chicago_democrat_office. That is recorded here, in that record, and in both research docs rather than being resolved by preference. METHOD: the modern West Upper Wacker Drive / North Clark Street intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 E 447648.5, N 4637409.7 (two nodes averaged, spread 14.3 m, fetched 2026-08-11); the origin sits 12.2 m east and 12.2 m south of it less the depth, so the north face is on the South Water frontage and the west face on the Clark frontage of a south-east corner lot. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M from the georeference, plus the 37 m the corner question is worth. The traced 1834 south bank runs 79.6 m north of this north face at this easting, which is 60 m more than the same measurement at Dearborn — local paper stretch and Wacker Drive's uneven build-out over the old dock line, not wharf depth. Facade bearing 0, north onto South Water, inferred from the street rather than from any statement. RECONCILED WITH THE COMMITTED PLAT 2026-08-24 (T-0127), AND THE CLAIM DID NOT MOVE — ONLY THE LINE IT WAS DERIVED AGAINST. The method above set this footprint's north face on the South Water frontage, and it found that frontage by taking the MODERN West Wacker Drive centreline out of OpenStreetMap and stepping 12.2 m south of it. That is not this project's own South Water Street: the committed centreline in data/streets/1835.json, offset by half the committed 80 ft corridor, is what tools/generate_plat_lots.py builds every platted block edge from, and it is the line every derived layer in this scene reads. Measured against it, this record's north wall stood 5.30 m OUT PAST the blk_south_water_clark frontage line, in the platted roadway — far enough into it that tools/generate_frontage_works.py refused the plank sidewalk along this stretch of South Water in writing and named this building in the refusal. THE REPAIR IS THIS RECORD'S OWN METHOD RUN AGAINST THIS PROJECT'S OWN LINE: the footprint is translated 6.80 m along the face's inward normal — dE -0.110 m, dN -6.805 m in local ENU, so UTM E 447660.7 N 4637389.9 becomes E 447660.59 N 4637383.095 — which leaves its north wall 1.50 m back from the committed frontage line, the same margin tools/generate_block_infill.py gives every reconstructed unit standing on this face. NOTHING ALONG THE STREET MOVED: the along-face position, the block, the corner and the side are untouched, and so is the confidence grade — re-deriving a coordinate from better geometry is not new evidence. WHAT IS STILL WRONG AND IS LEFT WRITTEN DOWN: the facade bearing stays 0 while this face runs at 0.93, so the front wall is 1.50 m back at its worst corner and up to 1.70 m at the other. That skew is smaller than the walk's own daylight and it is not corrected here, because rotating a documented record is a second claim and this one is a repair. THE CROSS STREET IS REFUSED, IN WRITING, WITH THE NUMBER (T-0195, 2026-08-27). The repair above answered South Water Street and could not answer this one, because a corner has two streets and the move that reconciles the frontage is along the other street's normal. Measured against the committed plat with tools/measure_corridor_intrusion.py, this footprint still laps Clark's corridor by 0.21 m — the fourth-shallowest lap any building in this town makes, and the deepest of the three corner residuals the South Water repair left standing. WHY IT IS NOT REPAIRED, AND THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDES IT. tools/measure_corridor_intrusion.py --escape bisects the shortest translation that takes each lapping record clear of the corridor it laps and reads that direction against the record's OWN facade bearing: here it is 0.213 m on a bearing of 90.36 degrees, which is 0.36 degrees off square to this facade — a slide SIDEWAYS ACROSS ITS OWN FRONT, not in or out of it. South Water's committed axis runs at 90.93 degrees beside this footprint, so that escape is a move ALONG South Water Street to within 0.6 of a degree. It would therefore change where along the business street this building stands, and the corner is the one part of this placement a source argues. Moving ACROSS the front is a different operation and is the one T-0127 defended: the setback is re-derived against a better line and the claim does not move. Moving ALONG it moves the claim. WHERE THE 0.2 M ACTUALLY COMES FROM, because it is not a mystery and should not be left as one. The method above stepped 12.2 m from an OpenStreetMap junction centre in BOTH directions. The South Water half of that offset was re-derived against this project's own committed centreline; the Clark half never was. Measured against the committed Clark centreline this record's west face stands 11.979 m out, where the platted half-width is 12.192 m — so the residual is the 0.221 m by which OpenStreetMap's junction centre and this project's committed Clark centreline disagree at this corner, and nothing else. AND WHY THAT IS NOT WORTH SPENDING A SOURCE ON. It is about 1.1 per cent of this placement's own stated working uncertainty of about 20 m, on a georeference carrying 17.5 m RMS (data/datum.json). Clearing it leaves the record clear of every platted corridor — the escape trades nothing away — and that is exactly what makes the temptation worth naming: the number would go to zero and the placement would be no more true. The lap is banked in tools/corridor_intrusion_baseline.json under `refused`, where the gate holds it at this depth and fails if it grows, and it may not outlive itself: if this corner is ever re-derived, the refusal has to be withdrawn with it.
placement.symbolic_location: The corner of Clark Street and South Water Street (today North Clark Street at West Wacker Drive); the south-east corner, which is this record's reading and not a statement in any source.

footprint.note: INVENTED — the parcel's borrowed rectangle, 12.192 x 7.62 m = 40 x 25 ft, taken from the Green Tree Tavern's attested frontage and room module because no source gives this building a dimension. The documented cap applies: South Water lots were 55 ft wide, so the frontage cannot have exceeded that. THE ONE FIGURE THAT MUST NOT BE USED IS THE ONE THE SOURCES DO OFFER. Andreas describes a THREE-STOREY building on this corner housing the Daily Chicago American on its third floor — in 1839, four years after the scene date, in a town whose first three-storey structure (the Saloon Building) is 1836 and is already in data/exclusions.json. Sizing or massing this 1835 record from the 1839 building would import the boom that had not happened yet.

stories.note: NOT ATTESTED FOR 1835 AND DELIBERATELY NOT TAKEN FROM THE 1839 DESCRIPTION. Andreas has a three-storey Harmon & Loomis building on this corner in 1839; the town's first three-storey structure was the Saloon Building of 1836, so three storeys in 1835 would be an anachronism this project already guards against in data/exclusions.json. Two is the reading: it matches Peck's documented two-storey frame store one block west and the Temple Building's documented two-storey frame at Franklin, which are the only two south-side commercial buildings whose height this dataset actually knows. One storey is possible. THE HONEST SUMMARY IS THAT THE 1835 HEIGHT OF THIS BUILDING IS UNVERIFIED, which is what this project's own dossier says.

construction.note: Not stated. Frame rather than log because this is a merchant's building on the town's principal commercial corner, and because the dossier records the 1835 south-side stock as overwhelmingly frame and log with no brick of consequence before 1837. Braced rather than balloon frame for the reason the Sauganash record gives: the two are not distinguishable from any word in the sources.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 5.5 m is about 18 ft, two 8 ft storeys plus floor structure and a sill course — the number this project uses for its other two-storey frame buildings. It inherits the storey count's uncertainty in full.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for frame buildings of this type, period and region. Typological derivation, not a measurement.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested for this building. 33 degrees is the frame_storefront archetype's own figure for a store, and it is adopted here rather than the 38 this project uses for taverns because the archetype argues the case from the dataset's one attested store footprint: a store's frontage is long and its plan shallow, so a tavern's pitch puts more roof above the eave than there is wall below it and the building stops reading as a shop. Inferred from construction practice and from the type, not measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested. One is the minimum for a store kept through Chicago winters. The COUNT is the inference; the stack's position, size and material are the archetype's, per docs/LIBERTIES.md L26.

dock.note: RECONSTRUCTED, UNDER THE OWNER'S RULING OF 2026-08-18 — 'you can add more docks!', given with the general instruction to be liberal with reconstructed items and label them as such (T-0062; data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/README.md). NO SOURCE STATES A DOCK, WHARF OR LANDING AT THIS FRONTAGE — that absence is exactly why this value is reconstructed and not inferred, one tier below the two river warehouses whose dock is stated in the dossier. What bounds the invention: (1) THE TRADE — a general merchant's corner store whose 18 November 1833 advertisement lists dry goods, crockery, hardware, wet and dry groceries, and a large lot of leather taken on commission — the class and weight of freight that comes off a vessel, not out of a wagon. (2) THE REACH — this building stands on the South Water river frontage between the forks and the Dearborn drawbridge, the working bank the 2026-08-18 brief shows crowded with masts (image 3) and the reach every schooner cargo landed on; a street of merchants whose whole stock came in by water did not work it over two landings. (3) THE PRACTICE — wharfing-out along the south bank is the practice T-0041's research note records as the thing that would move this layer off reconstruction, and the docks it drew are this landing's pattern. The landing itself is the wharf layer's standard form (data/wharves/river_landings.json, tools/generate_river_wharves.py), every dimension invented within the bounds L132 states; geometry 'simplified' is the exact claim — a standard-form landing stands for a statement this record cannot make from evidence. Claimed at docs/LIBERTIES.md L145. The Temple Building on the same frontage gets NO landing from the same rule: worship and a school take nothing off a schooner. STATED AND NOT YET DRAWN: the traced 1834 bank lines end at local E 390 and this frontage lies east of them, so tools/generate_river_wharves.py refuses the landing with that reason on the record (clause 4b) rather than standing a deck on an extrapolated endpoint. T-0106 owns extending the trace; when it reaches this reach the landing draws itself with no further authoring.

siding_exposure_m.note: INVENTED WITHIN A STOCK SET, NOT DERIVED. No source states the exposed face of any Chicago building's siding. The value is one of four period mill sidings — 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6 in to the weather; this record wears 5 in — dealt by tools/deal_siding_stock.py: keyed to the phase's construction season, because buildings sided from the same season's shipments of St Joseph sawn lumber tend toward one stock, then advanced so no frame building within 60 m shares this one's. The separation is the surface variety T-0049 reconstructs, not a claim about 1835. docs/LIBERTIES.md L148 owns the invention.

function.note: A general merchant's store. The contemporary advertisement of 18 November 1833 lists dry goods, crockery, hardware, wet and dry groceries, and 'on commission, a large lot of Leather, Saddlery, &c.' — the last of which makes the firm a commission house as well as a shop, which is what most of South Water Street was.

occupants.value: C. & I. Harmon, merchants; the firm Andreas names as Harmon and Loomis
occupants.note: A DISCREPANCY BETWEEN THE TWO SOURCES, RECORDED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED. Andreas names the concern 'Harmon's and Loomis's'. The advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is headed 'C. & I. HARMON' and names no Loomis. Those are compatible — a firm styled by the Harmon brothers in its own advertising and remembered fifty years later as Harmon and Loomis, or a partnership formed between 1833 and 1835 — but they are not the same statement and the record should not pretend they are. A SECOND POINT ABOUT THE SOURCE ITSELF: the transcription supplied with the scan reads 'C. & L. HARMON'; the scan reads 'C. & I. HARMON'. The scan is cited, not the transcription, and the same transcription's attribution of another advertisement in the issue is treated with the same caution in chicago_democrat_office.

residents.name: The Harmon brothers' household
residents.why: A DISCREPANCY CARRIED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED, and it is already on the building record: Andreas names the concern 'Harmon's and Loomis's' while the 1833 advertisement is headed 'C. & I. HARMON' and names no Loomis. Those are compatible - and note that Loomis is the brothers' own middle name and their mother's maiden name, Welthyan Loomis - but they are not the same statement.

persons.name: Charles Loomis Harmon
persons.note: THE INITIALS ARE RESOLVED BY A SENTENCE IN ANOTHER CHAPTER, which is the find that makes this household possible. Andreas's life of Dr Elijah Dewey Harmon lists his five surviving children: 'Charles Loomis Harmon, Isaac Dewey Harmon, Harriet Harmon, Lucretia Harmon, and Welthyan Loomis Harmon.' C. and I. are therefore the doctor's two eldest sons, and the firm in the town's first newspaper is a family partnership. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Harmon, C. L.” (poll_1834_051, line 220). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Harmon' agrees with the entry's forenames; 3 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Chas. L. Harmon” (f1839_v0709, printed page 40, ward 1). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Harmon' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins C. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 6 times, as “HARMON CHARLES L”, “HARMON CHAS L”, 1833-10-22 to 1836-06-30: 1 federal land entry — NW sec 04 T39N R13E and 4 lots in the platted town — lot 10 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIV (L10BL20CHIV, as printed); lot 7 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIV (L7BL20CHIV, as printed); lot 8 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIV (L8BL20CHIV, as printed); lot 9 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIV (L9BL20CHIV, as printed) and 1 parcel of the school section — BL137 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read, 80.45 acres stated in all, for $5540.55 (ls0227, ls1210, ls1211, ls1212, ls1213, ls0751). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $5310.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: HARMON CHARLES L matches Charles Loomis Harmon: the forename names Charles Loomis Harmon of the 6 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

residents.research_note: TWO BROTHERS IDENTIFIED BY CROSS-READING TWO CHAPTERS OF THE SAME BOOK, which is the kind of result this layer exists to produce: a newspaper masthead of initials becomes two named men with a father, a home town and a reason for being in Illinois. THE THIRD HARMON IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT. An Isaac Harmon was the town's clerk and collector in 1833-34 and is not written here, because Andreas's 1832 militia list carries two distinct Isaac Harmons and this project cannot tell which is which. That is a documented resident consciously left out of the count rather than guessed into it.

research_note: A STORE THIS DATASET KNOWS THE TRADE OF AND NOT THE BUILDING. The contemporary advertisement of 18 November 1833 tells us what Harmon sold; Andreas tells us the firm was on South Water Street by 1833 and that a Harmon & Loomis building stood at the corner of Clark and South Water. Every visible property of the structure — its side of the crossing, its size, its height, its material, its roof — is inference or invention, and the two that matter most are argued in full on the position and on stories. THE HEIGHT TRAP IS THE ONE TO WATCH: the vivid description available for this corner is the three-storey building of 1839 with the Daily Chicago American on its top floor, and 1839 Chicago is a different town. Chicago's first three-storey building was the Saloon Building of 1836, which this project already excludes by date. The 1835 height is unverified and this record says so rather than borrowing. THE CORNER TRAP IS THE OTHER: if Harmon & Loomis's building is the same building the Chicago Democrat rented an office in, this record is a duplicate standing 37 m east of chicago_democrat_office. That possibility is set out on both records and in docs/RESEARCH/harmon_loomis_store.md, and it is the single most likely way this parcel is wrong.
